label: Lost the story
title: The Dodo Was Framed!
dek: For 400 years, the dodo has been the world’s shorthand for fat, dumb and doomed. Nobody ever took its side. We reopened the file.
summary: The dodo’s reputation as fat, slow and stupid came from paintings, travel writers and taxonomists, not from anyone who saw a wild one.

blocks.text: THE FRAME JOB: Roelant Savery, Edwards’s Dodo, 1626. Natural History Museum, London. Painted from overfed captives. Copied for 300 years.
Everybody knows the dodo. Fat. Slow. Too stupid to run away. So dumb its name means “fool.” So gross that sailors wouldn’t eat it.
Almost none of that came from anyone who saw a wild one.

rows: Wild dodos weighed about 10 to 14 kilos, roughly a big wild turkey. The chubby ones in the paintings were overfed captives and badly stuffed specimens.
Its toe tendons match those of modern running and climbing birds. Researchers in 2024 called it almost certainly active and fast. Nobody ever timed one.
A 2016 scan of a dodo skull found a brain exactly the size you’d expect for a pigeon that big, plus an extra-large smell center. It wasn’t a genius. It was a perfectly normal pigeon.
The Dutch first called it walghvogel, roughly “tasteless bird.” In 1602, one crew caught about two dozen and salted the leftovers for later.

An English travel writer said so in 1634 and credited Portuguese sailors. The Portuguese left no known record of the bird. The earliest dodo-word on record is the Dutch dodaars, from 1602, which means something like “fat-arse.”¹ Wrong end.

blocks.text: THE DEFENDANT: As the bones say it looked: lean, upright, about the weight of a big wild turkey.
The suspects: none of them ever saw one alive in the wild

rows: Painted a plump dodo that became the standard image for centuries, copied by people who never saw a feather.
Gave us “dodo” and the “fool” story, sourced to sailors who never wrote it down.
Gave it the scientific name Didus ineptus. That’s Latin for “inept dodo.” Officially.
Put it in Alice, running a race where everybody wins. By 1886, “dodo” was slang for a dim person.
Built a famous dodo skeleton and posed it like Savery’s painting. It came out squat. He fixed it three years later.

blocks.text: Around 1625, an artist at the Mughal court in India painted a dodo: slim, brown and alert. Western scientists first saw it in 1958. By then everyone had already decided what a dodo looked like.
EXHIBIT A: c. 1625 · Mughal court. Attributed to Ustad Mansur. Institute of Oriental Manuscripts, St Petersburg.
~4,200 years ago: Survived. A drought killed more than 100,000 animals in a single Mauritius swamp, mostly giant tortoises and dodos. The dodo survived it.
1598: The Dutch arrive. Pigs, monkeys and rats came with them. Dodos nested on the ground.

1662: Last confirmed. The last confirmed dodos were seen on a tiny island offshore. Later “dodo” sightings may have been a different bird, the red rail, which had picked up the name. The dodo couldn’t even keep its own death certificate.
The experts had a rough few centuries too

items: Some 18th-century French naturalists decided the dodo was about as real as a griffin.

In 1977, a scientist argued in Science that a Mauritius tree couldn’t sprout without dodos. His evidence: he fed its seeds to 17 turkeys, and three sprouted. He had no comparison seeds. Young trees that sprouted long after the last dodo were already growing on the island.

blocks.text: The dodo lost the fight, and the fight was against pigs. It lost the story to a painter, a travel writer, a Swede, an anatomist and a math lecturer. None of them ever saw one alive in the wild.
“I was a perfectly normal pigeon. That’s all I ever wanted to be.”
¹ “Fat-arse” is the likelier origin, not a certainty. Edwin wanted that in a footnote. I wanted it in the headline. [H.C.]
